::: {.exercise-lead}
This exercise measures how easily people across Singapore can reach eldercare services, then compares three ways of expressing accessibility.
:::

## Introduction

Accessibility depends on both the supply of services and the distance people need to travel. The analysis uses a common origin-destination matrix to compare the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM methods.

### Learning Outcome

This exercise covers importing and preparing spatial data, reshaping an origin-destination matrix, calculating three accessibility measures, and comparing their spatial patterns.

## The data

Four datasets are used:

- `MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL`: Singapore's 2014 planning subzones.
- `hexagons`: 3,125 demand locations represented by 250-metre hexagons.
- `ELDERCARE`: 120 eldercare service locations.
- `OD_Matrix`: travel costs between every hexagon and eldercare centre.

The supplied demand and capacity values are simplified for learning purposes. Each hexagon is assigned a demand of 100 and every eldercare centre a capacity of 100.

## Getting Started


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pacman::p_load(tmap, SpatialAcc, sf, 
               ggstatsplot, reshape2,
               tidyverse)
```
:::

### Cleaning and updating attribute fields of the geospatial data

Only the identifiers needed for the analysis are kept. The constant demand and capacity values allow the comparison to focus on distance.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
eldercare <- eldercare %>%
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) %>%
  mutate(capacity = 100)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagons <- hexagons %>%
  select(fid) %>%
  mutate(demand = 100)
```
:::


## Apsaital Data Handling and Wrangling

### Importing Distance Matrix

The origin-destination table contains one row for every hexagon-facility pair. `total_cost` combines the entry, road-network and exit distances.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ODMatrix <- read_csv("chap17/data/aspatial/OD_Matrix.csv", skip = 0)
```
:::


### Tidying distance matrix

The long table is widened so each row represents one origin and each column one eldercare destination.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distmat <- ODMatrix %>%
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) %>%
  spread(destination_id, total_cost)%>%
  select(c(-c('origin_id')))
```
:::


The costs are converted from metres to kilometres before modelling.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat/1000)
```
:::


## Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using Hansen Method

### Computing Hansen’s accessibility

The Hansen method considers every eldercare centre but reduces the contribution of facilities that are farther away.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2, 
                            family = "Hansen"))
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```
:::


Results below use `power = 2`. The compact version is kept as an unexecuted example of a gentler distance decay (`power = 0.5`).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 0.5, 
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
```
:::


### Visualising Hansen’s accessibility

#### Extracting map extend


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mapex <- st_bbox(hexagons)
```
:::



::: {.cell fig_width='12'}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(hexagon_Hansen,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: Hansen method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-exercise-07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


### Statistical graphic visualisation

The planning-region field is added to each hexagon so the accessibility distributions can be compared by region.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon_Hansen <- st_join(hexagon_Hansen, mpsz, 
                          join = st_intersects)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data=hexagon_Hansen, 
       aes(y = log(accHansen), 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-exercise-07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using KD2SFCA Method

### Computing KD2SFCA’s accessibility

KD2SFCA uses a five-kilometre catchment and balances service capacity against the demand that competes for it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km, 
                            d0 = 5,
                            power = 2, 
                            family = "KD2SFCA"))

colnames(acc_KD2SFCA) <- "accKD2SFCA"
acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)
```
:::


### Visualising KD2SFCA’s accessibility


::: {.cell fig_width='12'}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(hexagon_KD2SFCA,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accKD2SFCA", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: KD2SFCA method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

### Statistical graphic visualisation


::: {.cell}


## Modelling and Visualising Accessibility using Spatial Accessibility Measure (SAM) Method

### Computing SAM accessibility

SAM also uses a five-kilometre catchment but applies its own adjustment for supply, demand and distance.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
acc_SAM <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                         eldercare$capacity,
                         distmat_km, 
                         d0 = 5,
                         power = 2, 
                         family = "SAM"))

colnames(acc_SAM) <- "accSAM"
acc_SAM <- as_tibble(acc_SAM)
hexagon_SAM <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_SAM)
```
:::


### Visualising SAM’s accessibility


::: {.cell fig_width='12'}

```{.r .cell-code}
tm_shape(hexagon_SAM,
         bbox = mapex) + 
  tm_polygons(fill = "accSAM", 
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                style = "quantile",
                n = 10,
                values = "brewer.blues")) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.3,
          fill = "red",
          col = "black") +
  tm_title("Accessibility to eldercare: SAM method") +
  tm_layout(frame = TRUE) +
  tm_compass(type="8star", size = 2) +
  tm_scalebar() +
  tm_grid(alpha = 0.2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-exercise-07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


### Statistical graphic visualisation


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
hexagon_SAM <- st_join(hexagon_SAM, mpsz, 
                       join = st_intersects)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data=hexagon_SAM, 
       aes(y = accSAM, 
           x= REGION_N)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(stat="summary", 
             fun.y="mean", 
             colour ="red", 
             size=2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](hands-on-exercise-07_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=960}
:::
:::


## Some other observations

- The darkest hexagons appear mostly around groups of eldercare centres. The far western and eastern edges remain lighter across all three maps.
- KD2SFCA produces sharper local changes because a facility stops contributing once it falls outside the five-kilometre catchment.
- One Central Region hexagon has a much larger SAM value than the rest. It stretches the vertical scale and makes the other regional boxes look flatter.
- Each map uses its own quantile breaks. The shades show relative ranking within a map, so the same blue does not represent the same accessibility value across methods.

## Takeaways

The three methods start with the same facilities, demand points and travel distances. Their maps differ because they treat distance and competing demand differently. Hansen gives every facility a distance-based weight, while KD2SFCA and SAM use a five-kilometre catchment. Comparing the locations of high- and low-access areas is clearer than comparing the raw values.
